w:r.w:t: Architecture · Design Patterns · Class Diagrams · Performance

This document specifies how Space Crusade is implemented in Unity. It translates the gameplay design documents into architecture decisions, design patterns, class structures, and performance strategies. Read alongside the Requirements Document and Design Volumes I–V.
All eight architecture decisions are recorded here as a quick reference. Each decision is documented in full in the section that follows.
Hybrid — pure C# simulation + MonoBehaviour view layer
Keeps simulation testable and engine-agnostic while using Unity for rendering and input.
Event bus (discrete) + shared state with explicit tick order (continuous)
Right tool for each job. Events for "something happened", shared state for "things are running".
Accumulator pattern — 20Hz fixed tick, interpolated visuals
Deterministic simulation decoupled from frame rate. Smooth visuals at any FPS.
Custom chunk grid — simulation radius + view radius
Factory simulates in loaded chunks. Views only spawned in view radius. Scales to planet size.
LOD ticking + GPU instancing for Swarmers
Swarm AI at 1–20Hz by distance. Swarmer meshes GPU instanced. Scales to hundreds of enemies.
GPU instancing for machines + chunk mesh merging for structural
50 block types = 50 draw calls. Structural walls merged per chunk. Scales to megafactories.
Newtonsoft JSON with versioning and atomic writes
Human-readable during development. Version migration built in from day one. Corruption-proof writes.
Flow fields for enemies + per-chunk NavMesh for droids/vehicles
One flow field serves all enemies per target. NavMesh for complex droid routing.

Space Crusade uses a strict two-layer architecture. The simulation layer contains all game logic as pure C# with no Unity dependency. The view layer is Unity — MonoBehaviours, GameObjects, renderers, animators, and input. The two layers communicate through a thin interface.
Block placement, construct membership, power balance, logistics item movement, machine production, enemy AI, combat damage, progression tracking, save/load serialisation.

SimulationView reads simulation state. EventBus carries discrete events upward. InputService translates Unity input to simulation commands.

The simulation is the Model. Unity GameObjects are the View. The View reads from the Model every frame to update visuals. The Model never reads from the View. This is strict — any violation creates untestable code.
├── Simulation/ # Pure C# — no Unity dependency
├── Shaders/ # GPU instancing, belt spline shaders
└── Tests/ # Unit tests against simulation layer only
The simulation is created and owned by a single MonoBehaviour that acts as the bridge between Unity's lifecycle and the simulation loop.

These are the rules that keep the game running at 60fps as the factory and battlefield scale. Every new system must be evaluated against them.
GetComponent is a hash lookup — expensive in hot loops.
Cache references in Awake() or Start(). Use [SerializeField] for inspector-assigned references.
No per-frame memory allocation in simulation tick
GC pressure causes unpredictable frame spikes.
Use object pools for enemies, projectiles, particles. Use structs for event types. Pre-allocate lists with capacity.
LINQ allocates enumerators on the heap.
Use for loops over arrays in simulation tick. LINQ is fine in editor code and one-time operations.
Belt simulation only ticks occupied slots
Empty belt cells must not tick.
Maintain a list of occupied slot indices per belt. Only iterate those.
Enemy AI ticks at distance-scaled frequency
LOD tick system (Section 5.3) is mandatory. Never add a per-frame enemy Update().
Chunk mesh rebuild is deferred and async
Rebuilding a chunk mesh blocks the main thread for several frames.
Mark chunks dirty. Rebuild on a job thread. Apply the new mesh at start of next frame.
Field rebuild for a large world grid is expensive.
Mark fields dirty on block change. Rebuild on background task. Never rebuild synchronously on main thread.
All instanced renderers batch per type
One draw call per block/enemy type is the target.
Never create a MeshRenderer per block. Route all block rendering through BlockInstanceRenderer or ChunkMeshBuilder.
Enemies, projectiles, belt items (as view objects), and particle effects must be pooled. Instantiate and Destroy are expensive — pooling eliminates runtime GC.
Power network recalc, chunk mesh rebuild
